newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU WILLING TO SELL WHEAT BUT NOT IN BIG VOLUMES.
newsitem.headline: EU WILLING TO SELL WHEAT BUT NOT IN BIG VOLUMES.

text.p: The European Union, which has agreed to sell wheat while raising export taxes in a compromise with the grain trade, said on Thursday it would be a regular exporter but would block any major export bids likely to disrupt local markets.

An EU farm official told Reuters the Commission's decision overnight to double a tax on soft wheat exports, to six Ecus per tonne, would halt strong demand for export licences at least for the rest of Thursday, but was not meant to prohibit all sales.

"What we want is calm and balanced management of exports, as regular a presence as possible, not a 'stop-and-go' effect or a big chunk of volume which would disrupt internal markets," said the official, who is close to EU grain export decisions.
"If we got export bids for 1.5 million tonnes they would not be accepted; that's obvious," he said.
The EU has been under grain industry pressure since Friday to meet demand for export licences as world prices move in and out of line with each other and the dollar helps European trade.
Even a 0.5-Ecu-per-tonne export tax did not prevent bids for over a million tonnes and the Commission hoped on Monday to calm the market by vetoing them and hiking the tax to three Ecus.
As more dollar gains eroded the higher tax, traders tried again over two days for 472,000 tonnes. The EU has now accepted these bids but is also doubling the tax again to six Ecus.

A Commission spokesman said Thursday's latest hike was meant to reduce the demand for export licences. Traders said it helped to push French wheat around $10-12 per tonne above competing U.S. soft red winter prices.
But the farm official said the six-Ecu tax was not a blunt signal the EU was out of the world wheat market. "Six ecus is dissuasive today but perhaps it won't be in 48 hours," he said.
This is in contrast to the prohibitive taxes slapped on wheat when the EU first decided to end 20 years of export subsidies and preserve local supplies 18 months ago.
"Our aim is not to prevent exports. There is no export ban," the official said.
He would not be drawn on what volume of export bids might be enough to bring the shutters back down. "I won't say that because then it becomes too complicated to manage," he said.
But he believed traders did have some latitude to complete their deals with the licences already in the market.

Traders, who must have a licence to export grain, have been bidding at fixed tax rates through a daily channel which usually serves as a backstop to weekly tenders for licences. The next tender is not until August 14 because of holiday schedules.
